articles.title: A power struggle in Iran could decide when Trump’s war ends
articles.summary: Iran’s internal power struggle could decide when Trump’s war ends
articles.body: More than four decades ago, after months of setbacks in the war against Saddam Hussein’s Iraq, thousands of young Iranian troops launched a surprise offensive that turned the tide. But rather than consolidate victory, the then-supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, wanted more: To topple the Iraqi dictator, who was drawing increasing support from Washington, and demonstrate to future enemies that war with Iran will exact a heavy cost. The Iraq conflict was pivotal moment in shaping the modern Iranian state. Khomeini’s decision turned it into a six-year war of attrition that killed hundreds of thousands, one of the bloodiest conflicts in the region’s modern history. And now, years on, the question of whether to press on or cut a deal is once again facing Iran. The revolutionaries who led the offensive dominate the seats of power in Tehran. To them, the current US-Israeli war, like the conflict with Iraq, was an imposed war whose outcome would not be determined by which side was most powerful – but which one would endure. On the other side, a more moderate camp senses a chance to consolidate Iran’s gains in talks that have made little progress. After six months of war, the deadlock has left the Islamic Republic bitterly divided, while its ultimate arbiter, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, remains in hiding. Winning the peace Tehran’s competing politicians maintain publicly that Iran has emerged triumphant in the war. Yet, a deep ideological schism remains over what victory for the Islamic Republic should look like. On one side stand pragmatists and technocrats led by President Masoud Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. They back a conclusive agreement, pointing to a war-battered economy, an exhausting US naval blockade and damage to the nation’s infrastructure. They have publicly warned that the window to settle the conflict from a position of strength is closing. They speak for Iranians who believe that ending the 47-year conflict with Washington is the surest way to ease the country’s domestic crises and keep the Islamic Republic alive by breaking its global isolation. “The war must end at some point,” Pezeshkian said this month. “It would be better to end it today, while we are in a position of strength and dignity, and the entire world acknowledges our victory.” On the other side stand hardline conservatives. Their ideology centers around a distrust of a Washington they see as hell-bent on destroying the Islamic Republic. For more than half a century they’ve warned against US intentions, and now they stand vindicated against their moderate opponents by Trump’s war. They also accuse sitting officials of being “Western-oriented” and of trying to influence public opinion toward a deal by exaggerating domestic issues. “They see the US as a deeply untrustworthy actor… and (have) been burnt so many times by Trump himself that they think that this is exactly what will happen again,” Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa program at London’s Chatham House think tank told CNN. “In their minds, by not losing (the war), they’ve won, and they’re not just trying to win out with a better deal from Washington, but they’re looking for internal longevity in their competition with their opponents.” They see Pezeshkian as a weak president who took office by chance after his hardline predecessor died in a helicopter crash. And his signature beside Trump’s on the June ceasefire agreement has ostracized him further, empowering their campaign to blame him for the shattered economy and the failed deal with Washington. So deep are the divisions that hardliners have accused officials of deliberately mismanaging the economic crisis to pressure an exhausted public into accepting a deal. Some allege that the government has engineered fuel shortages to make an agreement unavoidable, others go further, accusing moderates of staging a coup. “Economically, are we really in a dead end, or are you just projecting a dead end?” asked hardline lawmaker Mohammad-Manan Raisi. “It has all been blamed on the war, while it is not all related to the war.” What do the hardliners want? The hardliners point to failed past deals with the US, including a nuclear agreement signed in 2015 with the Obama administration that Trump later tore up, and they cite the two times that the US attacked the Islamic Republic amid negotiations. This camp wagers on the Islamic Republic’s endurance, and claim that a policy of confrontation supported by armed regional proxies, missiles, drones and Shia religious belief has guarded the country more effectively than the diplomacy championed by the “Western-oriented” politicians. “Hardliners concluded they will achieve no deal with Trump and perhaps they’re now just living in the war between the wars,” Vakil said. “They think that they can wear Trump down and they can play for time to weaken him by extending economic pain.” A hardline lawmaker described those advocating for a deal with the US as standing against former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei – killed in US-Israeli strikes at the beginning of the war. “They want to prepare public opinion to accept an agreement and a humiliating peace,” Kamran Ghazanfari told parliament on Thursday, referring to those in favor of diplomacy with the US. “Yet the enemy has repeatedly shown that no matter how many concessions we make to it, no matter how much we retreat before it, it will never be satisfied and will continue to demand other things from us, and it will settle for nothing less than our complete surrender.” ‘Trump isn’t helping’ As Iran’s pragmatists play a high-stakes poker game with Washington, hardliners’ warnings against a deal with the US have gained force amid an erratic strategy from Trump’s and uncertainty about his commitment to a potential agreement. “Trump is not helping. He says he wants to make Iran great again then threatens Iran in the next tweet, and that fans the flame of paranoia within the Iranian system,” Vakil said. The conservatives, who have elements controlling newspapers, state broadcasters, protesters on the street and followers in the military, believe Trump is using diplomacy to prepare for another military campaign and that “every time they go down the road of diplomacy” with Trump he “betrayed them,” she added. Mojtaba Khamenei has remained quiet amid the divide. It appears that he understands that choosing a side on negotiations with an unreliable Trump could harm his office just as he is working to secure legitimacy. On Friday, he praised the government’s performance under pressure but urged officials to address the country’s weaknesses without dwelling on them publicly, warning that doing so could embolden Iran’s enemies and demoralize its allies. With no one to rein them in, hardliners are pressing ahead with their campaign against a deal. “Our martyred Imam (Ali Khamenei) warned them dozens of times – how do they not understand?” said Ghazanfari about his domestic opponents. “They speak in a way that reeks of nothing but capitulation and surrender.” Additional reporting by Aida Karimi

articles.title: Rescuers pump air into hydropower tunnel in search for missing workers after Nepal-China flooding
articles.summary: Around 3,000 people are still missing after this week’s catastrophic flash flooding on the Nepal-China border. Follow live updates.
articles.body:
• Rescue effort: A search is underway more than 900 missing workers at various hydropower projects in Nepal after Wednesday’s catastrophic flooding. Emergency workers have pumped air and dropped food into one tunnel but have yet to establish communication with anyone inside.

• Search continues: More than 3,000 people are still missing. The US is providing $3.6 million of humanitarian aid , up from the earlier announced $500,000.

• Grim toll: The disaster has killed at least 750 people . More than 700 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal and at least 16 in China. Nepali authorities are struggling to cope with the mounting number of bodies, and Chinese officials have said their search teams have found no more survivors yet.

• New barrier lake: A landslide detected on Saturday evening created a new barrier lake on a river near the disaster zone, prompting the evacuation of rescuers in China, reported state media.

Family photos, spiritual statues, and reminders of his missing father: These are some of the things Sumit Nepal hoped to find when he returned to his home in Devighat searching for anything salvageable among the mud and debris that engulfed much of the village.

“But there was nothing left,” Nepal told CNN.

His father Navaraj, 42, remains missing. His last known whereabouts was meters from the China-Nepal border crossing that was engulfed in flood water earlier this week.

“Father where are you? Please be safe and contact us,” he said.

For now, all he has to remember his home in happier times is a photo of him and his father standing by the front door on a sunny day and another of him with his mother, inside on the stairs.

People cut off by flood damage in Nepal are in urgent need of clean water to prevent disease spread, according to an aid chief who raised concerns of damaged pipes and contaminated drinking sources.

“The biggest concern is that dirty water can spread disease, so people need clean water for drinking and washing as quickly as possible, alongside urgent help for those still stranded,” Sudarshan Neupane, country director of WaterAid Nepal, told CNN on Sunday.

“Besides, there is a real danger of disease outbreak from the decayed bodies and animals, as we have seen in other disasters.”

The immediate priorities are to rescue those still trapped, get clean water and essential supplies to affected families and restore electricity and water connections, Neupane said.

In the longer term, national and international financing is needed “to repair and strengthen damaged water systems, help communities prepare for future floods and reduce the risk of disease,” he added.

We’ve been continuing to report on search and rescue efforts after Wednesday’s deadly flooding near the Nepal-China border.

Survivors have begun returning to mud-caked homes to search for their belongings as relatives of those missing are still desperately searching for updates on their loved ones.

Death toll climbs: At least 750 people have died in the disaster. In China, 16 people were killed and 546 people are missing, according to authorities on Sunday local time. Chinese officials added that no more survivors have been found yet. Eighteen Americans are among the at least 261 foreigners missing in China. In Nepal, at least 734 died with 2,498 missing.

Rescue efforts: Rescuers have been using heavy equipment to clear debris in tunnels at hydropower projects along the Trishuli river, where about 900 employees are still missing . They have pumped air and sent food through holes bored into the tunnels.

New barrier lake: A landslide on Saturday evening created another barrier lake near the Nepal-China border, prompting the evacuation of rescue personnel near Gyirong Port, Chinese state media reported.

US aid: The State Department said the United States is providing $3.6 million of humanitarian aid to Nepal, up from the $500,000 it announced earlier. It includes emergency food assistance for up to 10,000 flood-affected households, the State Department said.

Victims’ burial: Workers are preparing a mass burial site in Nepal’s Chitwan region. Footage from a CNN team on the ground showed workers in hazmat suits placing body bags into the back of a van.

An American citizen said he feels “super happy and lucky to be alive” after he narrowly avoided the flash floods in Nepal.

47-year-old Roman Shteynshlyuger is now in the US after returning from Nepal, where he was supposed to join a trekking tour to Tibet. He said he dropped out of the tour after his Chinese visa was denied.

Shteynshlyuger went to hike Everest Base Camp instead, then flew to the US. He joined a party for his mother’s 70th birthday in Brooklyn on Saturday, and said he felt “unimaginable joy and happiness to be here.”

“I’m glad I wasn’t there, but I feel sad for the families,” he said. “It was shocking.”

He had been on a list of “missing” American passport holders in the flood, but he has now informed the authorities that he is safe.

In an email seen by CNN, Nepal Tourist Police responded saying “we are so glad to hear this news,” adding “have a great and prosperous life ahead.”

Shteynshlyuger moved to the US from Ukraine in 1991, and has been living in Puerto Rico in 2020. His family lives in Brooklyn.

A 13-year-old Nepali girl told CNN she was nearly washed away by the floods as she rode on her school bus to safety.

“At first, the teachers knew that a big flood was coming,” 13-year-old Rojina Bhatta said. “They instructed us to leave the school and go to a safe location.”

The driver “drove extremely fast” and got them to safety, she said, after picking up some other students on the way.

“The water was chasing us,” Rojina recounted. “Everyone on the bus was scared and crying.”

Her school, Trishuli High School, was completely washed away in the flood. But the driver managed to save around 50 children on the bus.

“When I recall that terrifying moment, I still get scared,” she said.

Bhatta’s father, Rajendra Bhatta, witnessed the flooding from near their home in Bidur, seeing dozens of homes washed away, along with a bridge and a newly-built road.

“The water in the river was roaring as if it were flying,” 38-year-old Bhatta said. “I saw it jumping into the sky.”

“Not just me, but my father and grandfather also never witnessed such a devastating flood in their lifetimes,” he said.

Bhatta has 30 buffalo across the river, which he now can’t access due to the bridges being destroyed. But he’s just grateful his family survived.

For the first time, Chinese authorities on Sunday provided a breakdown of the nationalities of foreigners missing in the Tibet region following the flooding disaster on the Nepal-China border.

261 foreign nationals from 23 countries are missing:

3 each from Russia, Malaysia and Germany

2 each from the Netherlands, New Zealand, Estonia, France and Ireland

1 each from Finland, Lithuania, Portugal, Ukraine, Spain, Hungary and Kazakhstan

Rescue teams are facing challenging conditions as they race to rescue workers in tunnels of hydropower plants, with water levels of the nearby river rising once again early Sunday morning local time.

“The water level of Trishuli River increased by 5 to 10 meters due to floods at the planned site again at around 4 a.m. today,” said the Nepali prime minister’s office on Sunday, referring to the Upper Trishuli 3A hydropower plant.

“The flood has started to cut the river banks off,” it said. “Road access to tunnel has been blocked and preparations are underway to make helicopter landing possible and recover important equipment.”

The office added that crews were using heavy equipment to remove debris, and that a special force is preparing to recover parts of the hydropower facility, its CCTV cameras, and other equipment.

Some viewers may find this footage distressing.

Workers are preparing a burial site in Nepal’s Chitwan region after Wednesday’s catastrophic floods.

Footage from a CNN team on the ground shows workers in hazmat suits placing body bags into the back of a van on Saturday night.

In another scene, diggers broke into the earth to prepare a mass burial site.

More than 700 people have died in Nepal and at least 16 have been killed in China.

Local police previously told CNN Chitwan officials are planning to bury hundreds of unidentified bodies in a mass grave at a sacred Hindu site. Authorities are struggling to cope with the number of already decomposing bodies.

A landslide on Saturday formed a new barrier lake on a river near the China-Nepal border, prompting rescue personnel near the Gyirong Port to evacuate, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported.

A monitoring drone detected the landslide Saturday evening on a mountain slope about 2.8 kilometers (1.7 miles) downstream from an existing barrier lake on the Purepu Tsangpo River, according to China’s Ministry of Emergency Management.

The latest landslide created a new blockage in the river and formed another barrier lake, authorities said.

Rescue teams at a hydropower plant in Nepal are sending food into a tunnel through holes bored by machines as they search for possible survivors inside.

More than 930 workers are unaccounted for at various hydropower projects in the flood zone in Nepal.

At the Trishuli–3A project, rescue workers have worked through the night as they try establish contact with anyone who might be inside the projects tunnels –– which stretch more than four kilometers according to documents from the Nepal Electricity Authority.

“Of late, two holes (were) created to send oxygen, light and food,” said Mohan Shakya, spokesperson at the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, on Sunday morning.

“Efforts are underway to rescue people by breaking the tunnel from other ways. We are sending more drilling equipment and explosive items.”

He added that Chinese and Indian teams, who arrived in the country on Saturday, are helping the rescue effort at the tunnel. “We haven’t stopped the work even in the night,” he said, adding that work continues even with light rain in the area.

The number of people confirmed dead after the Nepal-China flooding has reached 750, with more than 3,000 people still missing, according to official tallies from Nepal and China on Sunday.

Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll there had climbed to 734, from a previous total of 670. At least 2,498 people remain missing in Nepal, including 589 foreign nationals.

Earlier on Sunday, Chinese authorities confirmed at least 16 people had died on in the Tibet region, with 546 people missing. Among them are at least 261 foreigners including 18 Americans.

Chinese authorities held a press conference on Sunday, sharing updates and details about rescue operations after catastrophic flooding hit Gyirong Port in Tibet.

The death toll rose to 16 while the number of missing fell to at least 546. At least 261 foreigners are among the missing, including 18 US citizens.

No more survivors have been found yet in China.

Chinese state media reported on Saturday that two villagers had been rescued.

Footage from Wednesday’s disaster showed the deluge engulfing a large administrative building at Gyirong Port. A rescue team leader previously told CCTV: “The buildings within the mudslide’s impact zone have largely been flattened, with no discernible outline of any structures.” The rescue team said they had seen no signs of survivors at the border checkpoint.

A barrier lake formed near the flood zone at the Nepal-China border from an initial landslide has overflowed, but the situation is stable.

“The barrier lake has already overflowed and started to discharge water,” officials said.

“Currently, the overall situation is stable and the possibility of a complete breach is relatively low.”

CNN’s Simone McCarthy and Laura Sharman contributed reporting.

Rescuers are urgently pumping air into into a tunnel at a hydropower project along Nepal’s Trishuli river, and plan to drill a manhole in the hopes of sending teams inside to look for survivors.

About 900 workers at various hydropower projects are unaccounted for, according to the country’s Independent Power Producers’ Association. About 361 workers have been rescued so far, their data shows.

“There has been some success in the ongoing rescue efforts at the Trishuli–3 ‘A’ Hydropower Project tunnel, which was buried under mud and sludge following the flood,” wrote Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, Nepal’s Minister of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, in an update late Saturday night.

Crews had been working with excavators to clear the mud and sludge, and had drilled a 6-inch hole through the upper section of the tunnel, he wrote. Initial inspections showed no debris inside; they’ve since pumped air into the tunnel, and let in light and sound, but have yet to establish communication with anyone inside.

Earlier on Friday, the Nepali army released dramatic video showing rescuers saving several people from the tunnel of a hydropower plant in Rasuwa district, with survivors crawling through thick mud and being carried out by emergency responders.

The Nepali army has released video showing rescuers saving several people from the tunnel of a hydro power plant in Rasuwa. The footage shows survivors crawling through thick mud to reach rescuers.

The Nepali government has requested experts on tunnel rescues from India and China to help free the trapped workers. Teams from both countries arrived in Nepal on Saturday.

The United States is providing $3.6 million worth of humanitarian aid to Nepal after disastrous flooding, the State Department announced Saturday — up from the $500,000 it announced two days ago.

The department said the US embassies in Nepal and China “are working closely to assist Americans and support disaster relief efforts.”

The State Department announced Thursday that the US was “quickly deploying” $500,000 in assistance to affected communities.

Living in the shadow of the world’s spectacular, ice-capped mountains has always carried dangers , but the devastating flood wave that carved a path of destruction on the Nepal-China border this week shows how life for the millions worldwide who live downstream of these peaks is becoming more unpredictable and more deadly.

Nepal is a country of jagged, towering peaks with sheer slopes sweeping down to narrow valleys, cut through by powerful rivers. Its stunning landscape attracts hordes of tourists; it’s also treacherous.

Nestled in the rapidly warming Himalayas, the country has long been a hotspot for flooding and landslides. But what happened on Wednesday “was of significantly larger scale than what we have seen in the recent past,” said Prashant Baral, a cryosphere analyst at ICIMOD, a Nepali climate organization.

An enormous chunk of glacier around 2,000 feet wide sheared off Langtang Lirung mountain in northern Nepal, accompanied by landslide, according to satellite analysis. It sent a deadly mix of ice, water, rock, sediment and boulders the size of cars crashing 7,000 feet downward, causing such a powerful tremor, it was initially mistaken for an earthquake.

This torrent – described by some as “ liquid concrete ” – surged through narrow gorges, wiping out homes, buildings, power plants, bridges and roads.

Scientists are still unpicking the exact causes of the devastating flooding on the Nepal-China border, but what we know so far is that the disaster began when a vast chunk of glacier sheared off the mountainside on Wednesday .

The glacier chunk plunged around 1 kilometer (0.62 miles) into the valley below, according to a team of international scientists, which has been poring over satellite images and other data.

The US Geological Survey says the event created the equivalent of a 5.2-magnitude earthquake.

A glacier collapse alone would not have been enough to generate such an enormous amount of energy, “so there had to be something else involved,” said Daniel Shugar, a geologist at the University of Calgary in Canada, who is part of the scientific group. They believe a landslide likely happened at the same time.

Scientists say there is still work to be done to establish exactly what happened and what made the flooding so deadly.

“Figuring out where that water came from is is actually probably the hardest thing about all this,” Shugar added.

Two lakes that subsequently formed beside the site of catastrophic landslides sparked fears of fresh flooding and prompted both China and Nepal to briefly pause rescue efforts.

Nepal’s foreign minister told a press conference on Saturday that the country remained on high alert for fresh flooding risks.

“The river systems and downstream flood risk are being continuously monitored,” Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said.

“Our systems are on high alert for any additional fraud risks, and all required coordination is in place.”

articles.title: Hertfordshire nature reserves spot rare species during heatwaves
articles.summary: A wildlife trust says unusually hot weather and increased monitoring has led to interesting finds.
articles.body:
A wildlife trust said some species had been spotted in nature reserves this summer for the first time in years.

Volunteers for the Herts and Middlesex Wildlife Trust recorded a great white egret near Ware and more than 300 Chalkhill blue butterflies at Hexton Chalk Pit near Hitchin, where they also found a glow-worm for the first time in 25 years.

The trust said it was partly due to the unusually hot weather but also the result of increased surveying and monitoring in the county.

Senior reserves officer Dan Townsend said: "This summer we've had some extraordinary records, from species that haven't been recorded in Hertfordshire for decades to new discoveries for individual reserves."

The St Albans-based trust manages more than 40 nature reserves covering nearly 810 hectares (2,000 acres) in Hertfordshire and Middlesex.

It said grasshoppers had flourished during the hot summer, while butterflies had been able to complete their life cycle more quickly and emerge in large numbers.

By contrast, bumblebees and hoverflies had struggled, the trust added.

Its reserves have provided the setting for several significant discoveries by the Herts Invertebrate Project , which was set up in 2015.

At the end of June, the project visited Fir & Pond Woods, near Potters Bar, and recorded Euides basilinea, a planthopper associated with reeds, which had no previous records in Hertfordshire.

At Aldbury Nowers, near Tring, the leafhopper Zygina hyperici was recorded for the first time in the county since 1916.

Arboridia parvula, a leafhopper associated with Common Rockrose, was also recorded for the first time in Hertfordshire since 1976. The survey also uncovered Agyneta mollis, a tiny nationally rare money spider.

Jersey Tiger moths, once more strongly associated with the Channel Islands, have increasingly been recorded further north, while Hummingbird Hawk-moths are also being seen regularly in Hertfordshire.

Townsend said: "These discoveries help us understand which species are present, where they are found and how they are responding to changes in their environment.

"That knowledge is essential for informing the management of our nature reserves effectively and giving wildlife the opportunity to thrive."

articles.title: Mapping Iran war’s strikes on Gulf energy – and what comes next for oil
articles.summary: US energy companies have reaped billions from rising oil price, but their assets in the region remain at risk.
articles.body:
Six months into the war on Iran, the largest US oil companies have posted their biggest profits since 2022, selling less oil at far higher prices. But the conflict is also putting their longstanding Gulf investments at risk, exposing the industry’s uneasy balance between wartime gains and mounting geopolitical vulnerability for investors worldwide.

Since the war began on February 28, Brent crude has risen about 22 percent, from $72 to $88 a barrel.

The Strait of Hormuz – through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas was shipped before the war – remains largely closed to commercial traffic, though Iran and Oman agreed last week on a temporary maritime route. Iran says the strait will not fully reopen until the United States fulfils its commitments under a lapsed interim peace deal, leaving longer-term security and management arrangements unresolved.

In the absence of a lasting resolution, the disruption is likely to continue supporting higher energy prices and creating windfalls for producers, despite placing energy companies’ regional assets and future projects at greater risk.

Rahul Choudhary, vice president of Upstream Research at Rystad Energy, an independent energy research company, said the conflict has already reduced the amount of oil and gas US energy firms are drawing from the Gulf region.

“Overall we expect US companies’ share of gas supplies [from the region] to fall by around 40 percent this year compared to last year [and] the share of oil supplies to drop by 30-35 percent,” he told Al Jazeera.

While higher commodity prices have helped offset the immediate financial impact, Choudhary said prolonged disruption is likely to delay major projects and weigh on the future growth plans of US oil and gas companies with a presence in the region.

The surge in the oil price since early March, when Iran first closed the Strait of Hormuz, has delivered a windfall for oil companies, but gains have been tempered by challenges in the Gulf.

Chevron has limited exposure to Arab Gulf supply disruptions, with the region accounting for just 5 percent of its total global output. The group reported its highest quarterly profit in six years of $12bn in adjusted earnings on July 31.

ExxonMobil, by contrast, has been far more exposed to disruption in the Middle East, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian attacks on US-linked infrastructure in the region affecting its operations in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which together account for 20 percent of its global equity upstream supply, according to Choudhary.

“We already saw in H1 [the first half of] 2026, the company’s upstream earnings dropped by around $1.3bn compared to H1 2025, due to lower upstream volumes from the Middle East. However, the shortfall was covered well by higher commodity prices,” Choudhary said.

The contrast highlights a broader divide between those US energy companies which have benefitted from tighter global supply – and the corresponding rise in the oil price – and those with assets, partnerships or operations in the Gulf at greater risk of disruption caused by recent attacks on energy facilities.

Where are US energy companies exposed in the Gulf?

The Gulf’s energy sector is dominated by state-owned giants such as Saudi Aramco, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) and QatarEnergy.

Although these national oil and gas companies retain control over the region’s reserves and core infrastructure, US energy firms have carved out strategic positions across the region.

US companies generate revenue through stakes in production assets, joint ventures, production agreements, refining and petrochemical projects, as well as through long-term contracts to provide equipment, engineering and operational expertise.

ExxonMobil has some of the largest US commercial interests in the Gulf.

The company has been a major partner in Qatar’s LNG sector for decades, holding stakes in several QatarEnergy LNG joint ventures linked to the expansion of the North Field. The field is the Qatari section of the North Field-South Pars structure, the world’s largest natural gas field, which Qatar shares with Iran, where it is known as South Pars. ExxonMobil also holds an interest in the UAE’s Upper Zakum offshore oilfield alongside ADNOC.

Similarly, ConocoPhillips joined the North Field East (NFE) and North Field South (NFS) expansion projects with QatarEnergy in 2022 to increase export capacity at Ras Laffan.

The US group, Occidental Petroleum, has become one of the largest foreign producers in Oman, operating the Mukhaizna heavy oilfield, the country’s biggest producing oilfield. It also holds interests in UAE gas and pipeline projects.

Chevron maintains a smaller but strategically important Gulf footprint. Through Saudi Arabian Chevron, the company operates oil assets in the Saudi-Kuwait Partitioned Zone, including the Wafra field. In July, it said it was exploring potential routes to move Iraqi crude to Mediterranean export terminals, which could reduce reliance on the Strait of Hormuz.

Where have attacks on energy facilities taken place?

According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), a US-registered independent conflict monitor, Iran and Iran-backed groups in the region have carried out at least 172 attacks on nonmilitary infrastructure across the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries since the US and Israel launched their war on February 28.

Energy infrastructure has been hit hardest, with oil and gas facilities, along with power plants and desalination plants, accounting for nearly half (48 percent) of all strikes on nonmilitary targets.

The UAE, Kuwait and Bahrain have suffered the highest number of successful strikes, with the majority aimed at oil and gas facilities.

Among the sites that have been struck are Kuwait’s Mina Abdullah and Mina al-Ahmadi refineries, the Bahrain Petroleum Company oil refinery, and ADNOC’s al-Ruwais Industrial City and the Habshan gas complex.

There have also been several strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities, most recently a drone strike on July 27 on the Abqaiq processing complex, one of the most critical nodes in Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure, processing more than seven million barrels of oil per day.

Nasser Khdour, Middle East assistant research manager at ACLED, said: “Oil and gas facilities, power plants and water desalination plants are likely to remain key targets for Iran because disruption to these sectors can increase economic pressure on Gulf states, while disruption to global energy supplies increases prices and pressure on the US during periods of escalation.”

In March, a drone attack close to the Saudi Aramco-ExxonMobil SAMREF refinery in Yanbu disrupted oil loading at the city’s Red Sea port. While the attack had only minimal operational impact, it highlighted the vulnerability of US-linked energy assets in the region.

Qatar’s Ras Laffan Industrial City, the world’s largest LNG export hub, which hosts major joint ventures between QatarEnergy, ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips, also came under repeated attack in March , at one point forcing the plant to halt production entirely. In June, an explosion as a result of a “ technical malfunction ” on Qatar’s Barzan gas project, where ExxonMobil holds a stake, killed at least 13 people.

“In terms of gas assets being impacted, major blows have been [dealt to] companies [that are] part of LNG projects in Qatar: ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips,” Choudhary said.

He added that ExxonMobil’s share of LNG supply from Qatar is expected to fall significantly this year to about four million tonnes compared with 13 million tonnes last year, while ConocoPhillips has also experienced reduced volumes to one million tonnes this year compared with 2.5 million tonnes last year.

The attacks on Qatar’s LNG infrastructure could have longer-term consequences. Damage to LNG trains at Ras Laffan could take years to repair, according to QatarEnergy, while delays to Qatar’s North Field expansion projects could push back planned supply growth.

“The attack on LNG trains 4 and 6 at Rasgas damaged roughly 13 million tonnes of capacity, which will take anywhere between three to five years to come back online with a total repair cost estimate of around $3bn,” said Choudhary.

He added that the second most impacted gas project has been the Shah gas project in the UAE, in which Occidental Petroleum has a 40-percent stake and where drone attacks in March caused a fire at the gas plant that halted operations.

The conflict has also affected ExxonMobil’s oil interests in the UAE, Choudhary said. Production from Upper Zakum, where ExxonMobil has a 28 percent stake, was reduced between March and May when export routes were disrupted, limiting the ability to move offshore crude.

Beyond the UAE, the most significant impact on US companies’ oilfield operations played out in Iraq. A drone attack hit the Sarsang oilfield in March , followed by an explosion at one of its storage facilities in April , together causing damage to the field.

Looking ahead, Choudhary said higher prices could support cash flows, but prolonged conflict risks could threaten future growth. ExxonMobil’s $10bn Upper Zakum and Qatar LNG expansions could face delays, while ConocoPhillips remains exposed through investments in higher-risk markets, including its planned 42-percent stake in BP’s Kirkuk operations in Iraq.

“For companies like Chevron and Occidental Petroleum, whose presence are in less volatile countries like Israel and Oman respectively, the impact of escalations will not be as severe, as we have not seen significant disruption in these countries,” said Choudhary.

US oilfield service companies in the Gulf

Oilfield service giants, including US firms SLB (formerly Schlumberger), Halliburton and Baker Hughes, provide drilling technologies, equipment and operational expertise across the Gulf, supporting Saudi Aramco, ADNOC and QatarEnergy.

For oilfield service companies, the outlook is mixed, according to Chinmayi Teggi, energy research analyst at Rystad Energy, a research group. While higher oil prices and energy security concerns could lift demand over time, near-term margins remain under pressure from higher logistical costs, supply-chain disruptions and delayed projects.

“For the Big Three (SLB, Baker Hughes and Halliburton), the conflict continues to weigh on regional revenues,” Teggi told Al Jazeera, adding that second-quarter Middle East revenues were down 8-10 percent compared with the previous year across the three companies, while higher oil prices meant revenues were higher in other geographies.

However, a recovery in suspended operations and production could help drive growth into 2027.

For US companies, therefore, the Gulf remains both an opportunity and a risk.

“The impact on US companies will depend on the extent of exposure and countries in which these companies are present,” Choudhary said.

Their investments have secured US access to some of the world’s most important oil and LNG projects, but the conflict has exposed the risk of operating in a region where energy infrastructure has become increasingly vulnerable to geopolitical conflict.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly warned Iran against restricting access to the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that the waterway must remain open to global commerce.

But for companies with billions of dollars invested across the Gulf, the challenge isn’t just about keeping shipments moving – it is ensuring the infrastructure remains secure, they say.

articles.title: Teenager accused of killing mother and brother allegedly used ChatGPT to create stories about murdering his family: What prosecutors found online before the double homicide
articles.summary: US News: There was nothing unusual about the way the tragedy first came to light. A tutor arrived at a family home in Acton, Massachusetts, for an appointment..
articles.body: There was nothing unusual about the way the tragedy first came to light. A tutor arrived at a family home in Acton, Massachusetts, for an appointment. No one answered the door. The father could not reach his wife or children either. He called the police and asked them to check on his family.What officers found inside the house on Tuesday, August 11, turned a routine welfare check into a double-homicide investigation. The bodies of 45-year-old Sudha Venkatesan and her 14-year-old son, Siddharth Aravind, were found inside the home on August 11. Their 17-year-old son, Arjun Aravind, was missing. Within hours, police found him in his mother's car in nearby Wayland and arrested him.Now, the case has drawn attention far beyond the Massachusetts town because prosecutors say the teenager had recently been using the internet- including AI and ChatGPT- to search for and create “fictional scenarios” involving the killing of his own family.According to CNN, prosecutors said Arjun had used the AI chatbot to explore what they described as “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about killing his family. Middlesex County District Attorney Marian Ryan said investigators found that he had been creating Gothic-novel-style stories, developing characters and asking questions that appeared to relate to threats against his family.A welfare check that uncovered a family tragedyThe sequence of events began when a tutor arrived at the family's Martha Lane home and could not get inside. Arjun's father, who had been unable to contact his family, then contacted Acton police. Officers who went to the house found Siddharth on the first floor and his mother in the basement, according to prosecutors. Both had suffered obvious trauma.At a subsequent court hearing, prosecutors described evidence of a physical and violent struggle and said blunt-force trauma had been involved. The official cause and manner of death were initially awaiting findings from the medical examiner. Arjun was not at the house. Investigators said he had left in his mother's Honda Accord.The search ended early the following morning when Wayland police responding to an unrelated alarm spotted the vehicle in a parking lot. Arjun was inside and was arrested without incident, authorities said. Items found in the car were also said to correspond with the murder scene.What prosecutors say about ChatGPTThe most unusual detail in the investigation emerged after Arjun's arrest. Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan said the teenager had recently displayed what investigators considered concerning behaviour. This included internet activity and use of ChatGPT to explore “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” concerning the killing of his family.Ryan said the teenager appeared to be using the chatbot to develop fictional narratives, including Gothic-style stories and characters. Investigators believed some of those scenarios appeared connected to threats against members of his family.The detail has inevitably raised questions about the role of artificial intelligence in the case. But prosecutors have not said that ChatGPT instructed Arjun to commit the killings, nor have authorities established that the chatbot caused the alleged violence.That distinction is important. The investigation is examining Arjun's internet activity as part of a much larger picture of his behaviour and circumstances.Father had reportedly become concernedCourt proceedings have also shed light on concerns within the family before the killings. According to CBS News Boston, Arjun's father had become worried about his son's behaviour and internet activity and had begun hiding knives in the house. The precise reasons for those concerns, and whether they were directly connected to the alleged killings, remain part of the investigation.Arjun's defence lawyer, Debra DeWitt, has requested a psychiatric evaluation. She told reporters after his arraignment that the family had recently moved to Acton partly to provide a support system and schooling for the children.The teenager has pleaded not guilty.What charges does Arjun face?Arjun has been charged with two counts of murder, along with charges including assault and battery on a family or household member, assault and battery and offences related to the alleged unauthorised use and theft of a motor vehicle. He was held without bail following his arraignment. His next major court appearance, a probable-cause hearing, is scheduled for September 11.The case remains under investigation, and the allegations against Arjun have not been proven in court.A case that raises difficult questions about AIThe Massachusetts case is likely to fuel an already growing debate over how generative AI interacts with vulnerable or troubled users, particularly children and teenagers.But the facts available so far point to a more complicated question than whether an AI chatbot is responsible for a crime. Here, prosecutors say they discovered disturbing AI-assisted fantasies alongside other concerning behaviour. What remains unclear is how those thoughts developed, what role, if any, the technology played in the teenager's actions, and whether warning signs could have been recognised earlier.For now, the central facts remain stark: two members of an Indian-origin family in Massachusetts are dead, a 17-year-old family member has been charged with their killings, and investigators are continuing to piece together what happened inside the Acton home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Guernsey cruise passenger numbers still low amid visitor rise
articles.summary: Guernsey welcomed 81,681 visitors in the second quarter of 2026.
articles.body:
The number of cruise ships visiting Guernsey is still low compared to pre-pandemic figures, a coach company boss has said.

Hannah Beacom, managing director of Island Coachway, said cruises would be booked 100 days of the year, and booked up to two years in advance, but now they were looking at between 40 to 50 a year.

"It makes a difference to how you plan your season and prioritise resources," she said.

The latest quarterly travel and visitor accommodation bulletin said visitor numbers, excluding yacht and cruise ship passengers, have risen to 81,681, which was not far below pre-pandemic levels .

Beacom said: "We're all agile within the industry, everyone's diversified."

However, she said it had been the "most positive" she had been since the pandemic.

Beacom added: "It's been a long climb for us out of the Covid years.

"We can see in these figures how we've got most of the business back and wouldn't it be great to bring the cruise liners along with it."

Beacom said with most cruise ships docking on Sundays, when the shops were either closed or shut at 17:00 BST, there was not a lot to do.

She said cruise ship passenger numbers range from 250 to 5,000 and she did not expect the whole town to open for a small amount of visitors.

Beacom also said 25% of cruise liners, sometimes 100%, were all inclusive and on pre-booked excursions whether it was with a coach operators, going to Herm or Sark or local walks.

Charlie Walker, co-chair of the States' Tourism Advisory Board, said it was working with organisers to align the events such as VisitGuernsey's Seafront Sundays with same-day cruise liner calls to give visitors "something to do".

She also said the board could look at seasonal opening hours.

Walker said the island remained a "seasonal destination" at present, but the aim was to extend the season from March to October with more events.

"We're only just getting started," she added.

articles.title: The younger vinyl fans falling in love with their records
articles.summary: Record traders say they have noticed a shift towards younger buyers in recent years.
articles.body:
Younger people are helping the revival of traditional vinyl records, according to record dealers.

Roger Joffe, co-owner of Wanted Records and organiser of the biggest record fair in the south-west of England, held at the Bristol Beacon, said: "The youngsters are coming in and buying trance and dance music, but also trad jazz and Duke Ellington."

Joffe believes newer fans find the format appealing and want to hold something physically rather than streaming music.

Around 2,000 record-buyers are expected to attend his next show on 3 October.

How Massive Attack's legacy is changing festivals

In pictures: Forwards Festival and rare Blood Moon

"There's a whole pile of people who have either got everything they wanted or stopped buying, so they drop off," he said.

"CDs came and went in a big way, and lots of people abandoned their records when they were the big thing, but now they're trying to buy their discarded records back."

Joffe said as a result, a lot of 90s vinyl now goes for big money, even for bands which charted at the time, because CDs were more popular.

"A good example is Oasis; their original [vinyl] albums can go for over £200 because there aren't many of them," he said.

Lucas, 25, from Cheltenham, started buying records when he was 19, and now works at Badlands Record Shop, where he used to be a frequent customer.

His collection of 250 records has "spiralled" since taking a job there.

"There's so much music on streaming, and there's a nostalgia for something you haven't experienced originally," he said.

"Obviously streaming is convenient, but if you buy a record you support the artist and you support individual retail in a way that is more substantial than just listening to playlists.

"I do think young people are more conscious of that fact now."

Jacki Harvey, co-owner of Vinyl Realm in Devizes, said much recent trade had been from students who had received money from relatives after passing their GCSEs.

"There's a big group of young people who want to be different, and not go down the Taylor Swift route, which makes my job really hard," she joked.

"I think a lot of them are hearing things online and then going to buy the vinyl in person, but we get a lot of requests for American stuff, which is hard to find here."

She said her older customers are also downsizing their homes, and she has taken in several collections from customers selling houses to live on the nearby Kennet & Avon Canal instead.

Harvey said record shopping was more than just buying and the thrill of looking through boxes offers a "switch-off experience" to customers.

She said because of the revival, people selling their collections often expected them to be worth more, but warned there was an oversupply of mass-produced records by popular bands such as the Beatles and Elvis.

She added: "I advise people to put them on eBay and make money that way."

Chris Hawes, founder of Atlas Records near Taunton, said he believed the age demographic for record fans was getting younger.

He said: "I'm 29. Everyone that works for the business is under 32, and there's nine of us."

He said the current best-selling records were those which had always been popular.

"The one exception to that is when a modern song takes things to new heights - Kate Bush is an example," he said.

"When her track was in Stranger Things on Netflix, we saw that sell out overnight."

The most valuable recent sale was a 13-record set by David Bowie, Five Years 1969-1973. Although it was only released in 2015, it fetched more than £3,000.

articles.title: Hopes porpoise net recording from Cornwall can help stop deaths
articles.summary: Scientists hope a recording of an entangled porpoise can help them find ways of reducing deaths.
articles.body:
Scientists are hoping a recording of a porpoise trapped in a net could help them develop practical ways of avoiding marine animal deaths in the future.

Researchers from the University of St Andrews found their acoustic monitoring kit had recorded two harbour porpoises foraging near a static fishing net off the coast of Cornwall.

They said the porpoises appeared to be aware of the net but after becoming distracted, one had become entangled and could lift it but not escape.

Dr Jamie Macaulay, lead author of the paper documenting the event , said the insights gained could "be crucial" in developing nets which would be more noticeable and allow larger species to break free from.

Macaulay said bycatch, when species become accidentally entangled in fishing gear, is the single biggest direct human-induced cause of death in dolphins and porpoises worldwide.

"Observing an event in such detail obviously brings home the harsh realities of the bycatch problem," Macaulay, senior research fellow at the School of Biology and Scottish Oceans Institute, said.

"But this is a problem that the fishing industry and conservationists all want to solve."

He said the findings could inform further development of devices which send out warning sounds to scare certain species away.

The research unit's passive acoustic monitoring systems on the gill net captured the two animals exchanging distinct call types, which the team said could have been distress signals.

A paper written by Wildlife and Countryside Link said more than 1,000 cetaceans, including porpoises, die every year in the UK after becoming trapped in static fishing nets.

Cornwall Wildlife Trust said 27 dead dolphins and porpoises had been found on Cornish beaches in January as a result of getting caught in fishing nets.

Macaulay said static net fishing was an important part of the industry and the research was not about stopping them from being used.

He added: "What this work, combined with other research, helps us do is gain a greater understanding of how and why bycatch happens, which will help us develop and accelerate sustainable and practical evidence-based solutions to reduce it."

The marine conservation charity ORCA said there had been significant declines in the European population of harbour porpoises over the last 40 years.

It said they were under threat from chemical pollution, vessel traffic, underwater noise and the depletion of prey by overfishing due to their preferred habitat of shallow, coastal zones.

The primary threat for the harbour porpoise was the accidental capture in fishing nets, the charity added.

articles.title: Manhunt after woman, 22, killed and five injured in Swiss shooting
articles.summary: Swiss media reported shots were fired at a rave overnight, with all the victims in their twenties.
articles.body:
A manhunt is under way after a 22-year-old woman was killed and five others injured in a shooting which reportedly took place at a rave in northern Switzerland.

The woman died at the scene, police said. Those injured were four men and a woman aged between 24 and 27, all of whom are in hospital with injuries "ranging from minor to severe".

The force confirmed the shooting happened at an event at a horse racing track in Aarau, near Zurich overnight. A rave was taking place in the area into the early hours of Sunday.

Police said the perpetrator's identity and possible motives were unknown, as were the "exact circumstances" of the incident.

Local media reported that the force was alerted to the shooting around 02:30 local time (01:30 BST).

Swiss DJ Tekibo, who was performing at the rave, described the incident as "heartbreaking" in an Instagram story.

He said he had "lost an important friend" and was "still trying to process what happened".

An area around the racing track, the town's swimming pool and sports field has been cordoned off, with the public urged to stay away.

A large contingent of officers has also been deployed beyond Aarau "as a precaution", Aargau Cantonal Police said. An AFP journalist reported seeing armed officers deployed on the highway up to 30km (18 miles) from the site of the shooting.

Aarau is located some 46km west of Zurich and is home to approximately 23,000 people.

The force asked witnesses to submit photographs and video from the scene.

Images from Aarau early on Sunday showed a heavy police presence in the area, with an armoured vehicle seen blocking a road. Armed police and officers in riot gear could be seen patrolling the streets.

In addition to police and fire officials, the regional disaster response unit (KKE) was deployed, according to broadcaster SRF.

It also reported that a Swiss Army helicopter could be seen surveying the area in the early hours.

Switzerland has one for the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe, although violent shootings are rare and tighter controls were introduced in recent years.

articles.title: A 55-year-old Missouri official reached the 13,804-foot summit of Wyoming's highest mountain and signed its register; he then disappeared for 5 days before rescuers found him alive and severely dehydrated
articles.summary: US News: 55-year-old Missouri deputy attorney general who had been missing in Wyoming's rugged Wind River Range for five days has been rescued alive, shortly a.
articles.body: 55-year-old Missouri deputy attorney general who had been missing in Wyoming's rugged Wind River Range for five days has been rescued alive, shortly after search crews confirmed that he had reached the 13,804-foot summit of Gannett Peak. Shaun Mackelprang was found on Wednesday morning, 26 August, walking in a confused state and severely dehydrated near Scott Lake, about eight and a half miles from the nearest trailhead. Searchers from Sublette County Search and Rescue and Tip Top Search and Rescue gave him intravenous fluids at the scene before flying him by helicopter to a medical facility in Pinedale. The rescue brought an end to a multi-day search across one of the most remote mountain wilderness areas in the United States. The operation began after Mackelprang failed to return from a solo trip to climb Wyoming's highest mountain.A difficult climb to the summitAccording to Wyoming news outlet Cowboy State Daily, Mackelprang made the trip as part of his goal to climb the highest natural point in all 50 US states. Gannett Peak was the 45th summit on his list. He left on Thursday, 20 August, from the Green River Lakes Trailhead. He set up a campsite in the backcountry before making his final climb towards the summit on Friday, 21 August. Reaching Gannett Peak requires a difficult 35-to-50-mile round trip through rough terrain, including large boulder fields, steep snow slopes and fast-changing mountain weather. Mackelprang reached the 13,804-foot summit on Friday and signed the official peak register, a logbook kept in a protected container at the top. However, strong thunderstorms and quickly changing weather moved through the range during his descent. He became lost in the difficult alpine terrain.Search teams mobiliseWhen Mackelprang failed to return as planned over the weekend, his family became worried. His sister Sheila contacted authorities in Wyoming on Sunday, 23 August, starting the emergency search. Deputies from the Sublette County Sheriff's Office found Mackelprang's vehicle parked at the Green River Lakes Trailhead. This confirmed that he was still somewhere in the backcountry. The search soon expanded, bringing in ground teams, aerial drone crews and a specialised helicopter team from Tip Top Search and Rescue, a non-profit volunteer group based in western Wyoming. A major breakthrough came when other climbers who had reached Gannett Peak after Mackelprang provided photographs of the peak register. The photos showed that he had reached the summit before disappearing. This helped search coordinators focus on the area between the summit and his campsite. Sublette County Sheriff's Office spokesman Travis Bingham told Cowboy State Daily that ground crews searched different grid sections using information from hikers and other physical clues. “It was a ground team that was just clearing an area and came upon him,” Bingham told Cowboy State Daily. “There's not really one smoking gun thing that pointed us there. You just follow the clues.” Mackelprang's brother, Romel, said the climber may have become confused after walking towards another lake that looked similar to the one where he had originally camped. “They found him wandering at a lake that probably looks similar to the one that his tent was pitched at,” Romel Mackelprang told Cowboy State Daily shortly after learning he had been found. “We don't know.”Rescue and recovery in PinedaleDespite spending five days exposed to high-altitude conditions with very little water, Mackelprang was still able to stand and walk when ground teams found him at about 9:45 a.m. on Wednesday. He was flown to St. John's Health clinical facilities in Pinedale, where doctors treated him for severe dehydration, exhaustion, bruising and widespread skin injuries. By Thursday, 27 August, his family said his condition had improved significantly. From his hospital room in Pinedale, Mackelprang thanked the search teams who put themselves at risk to find him in statements published by Cowboy State Daily. He gave special thanks to Tip Top Search and Rescue and the Sublette County Sheriff's Office for being “ready and prepared to stand up for me in my time of need.” “It's no easy task to put your life on the line for someone else, especially a stranger who has no place in their lives,” Mackelprang said. “These women and men did so without a second thought. May God bless them for their good deeds and compassion.” Officials in Missouri also praised the search effort. Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway released a statement thanking the agencies involved in bringing her colleague home safely. “We are thrilled to hear that Deputy Attorney General Shaun Mackelprang has been located,” Hanaway said in a statement released to media organisations. “Our office is beyond grateful for everyone's prayers and the steadfast work of the Sublette County Sheriff's Office and drone team, Tip Top Search and Rescue's volunteers and helicopter crew, and Wyoming State leaders.”The dangers of Gannett PeakMountaineering experts consider Gannett Peak, along with Montana's Granite Peak, one of the hardest state highpoints to climb in the contiguous United States. Unlike mountains that can be reached by roads or short maintained trails, Gannett Peak requires a multi-day wilderness trip just to reach the base of the summit. Climbers must deal with loose rock and scree, hidden crevasses and sudden cold weather that can send temperatures below freezing even in late August. Mackelprang has worked in the Missouri Attorney General's Office since May 2021. He previously handled high-profile state legal cases before the Missouri Supreme Court. He remains in Pinedale recovering, while his family prepares for his eventual discharge and return to Missouri.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Search continues for boat and crew 'in distress' off Plymouth
articles.summary: Two of the five crew members on board are still unaccounted for, the coastguard says.
articles.body:
Rescue efforts are continuing for a vessel in distress in the English Channel as two crew members remain missing, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency has said.

A coastguard rescue helicopter, fixed wing plane and two RNLI lifeboats began searching an area south-west of Eddystone Lighthouse off Plymouth shortly after 18:00 BST on Saturday night.

In an update early on Sunday, HM Coastguard in Falmouth confirmed three of the five people aboard the boat had now been accounted for. It did not share further information about the vessel or the nature of the emergency.

A large number of civilian vessels were assisting the "intensive search", a HM Coastguard spokesperson added.

They also confirmed that an intensive search was maintained during the night.

"It is continuing today with multiple assets sent to help," they said.

Lifeboat crews from Newlyn and Salcombe have taken over the search from the Plymouth and Falmouth RNLI crews, who worked through the night.

A large area around the venue has been cordoned off and police have asked members of the public to stay away from the area. articles.title: Why London's ground will be slow to recover from the drought
articles.summary: London's clay ground will need sustained rainfall over a substantial period to fully recover.
articles.body:
London is still experiencing drought conditions and, despite recent rain, much of the capital's ground will take time to recover after weeks of record-breaking dry weather.

About 80% of London sits on clay, which extends to depths of more than 100m (328ft) in some places.

The clay has lost moisture, causing it to shrink and crack. In some cases, this can lead to subsidence, resulting in damage to buildings and homes.

Sustained rainfall over a prolonged period will be needed for the ground to fully recover, experts say. Rob Higginson, a geotechnical engineer, says it will be a "very slow process" and that "a single downpour is not going to do it".

July was the driest on record for England and Wales , and a hosepipe ban remains in place for Thames Water and Affinity Water customers in London following prolonged dry weather, low rainfall and increased demand for water.

Higginson said that while "putting a hose on the ground will keep your grass growing, it won't affect the underlying clay at all".

He explained how recent heatwaves had affected clay deep underground.

"If the clay gets warm, it loses volume, and it's going to go down and contract.

"You get the cracking, but you also get downward movement. If a house is sitting on top of the clay, it will go down with it."

He said this predominantly affects homes built between the post-war period and the 1980s.

However, even when rain does arrive, he said the recovery process would not be straightforward.

Higginson said: "The topsoil will absorb a certain amount of it, and then it will go down and sit on the clay layer.

"Then you've got surface runoff, so the excess water will just run off.

"What you really need is prolonged rain. It doesn't have to be intense, just a reasonable amount over a long period of time, so it has time to percolate into the very fine voids in the London clay."

Even when the grass begins to turn green again, the clay beneath may take much longer to recover from the effects of this summer's drought.

articles.title: American startup raises $180 million to drill rock over 5km deep to build world's first superhot geothermal plant at 500 °C
articles.summary: US News: Quaise Energy, an American startup, announced on August 27 the final closing of a $180 million funding round, which included $35 million from Nabors, .
articles.body: Quaise Energy, an American startup, announced on August 27 the final closing of a $180 million funding round, which included $35 million from Nabors, to finance the Obsidian Project in Oregon, where a microwave gyrotron will create wells in rock between 300 °C and 500 °C to establish the first commercial superhot geothermal plant on the planet, as per a report by ThinkGeoEnergy.According to the statement, the Series B totals $180 million, bringing the startup's total funding to $280 million since its inception. The first tranche, amounting to $134 million, was previously announced on July 7, led by Prelude Ventures with participation from Japanese companies JERA and Idemitsu Kosan. The new addition to the list is Nabors Industries, one of the largest oil and gas drillers in the world, which contributed $35 million and signed a strategic agreement. According to the release, Nabors will provide a dedicated land rig and integrate its reservoir modelling platform, well design, and drilling strategy into the project. In other words, the oil and gas industry is lending a rig, software, and personnel for a technology that promises to eliminate the need for a drill bit.Vaporising a rock without touching itA gyrotron is a millimetre-wave generator, a high-frequency microwave technology created to heat plasma in nuclear fusion reactors. According to MIT News, engineer Paul Woskov from MIT’s Plasma Science and Fusion Centre spent 14 years testing the concept of directing this beam downwards. His description is straightforward: these are very powerful beam sources, akin to lasers, but at a different frequency range.In practice, the beam travels down a waveguide to the bottom of the well, heating the rock to the point of melting and vaporising it without mechanical contact. There is no rotating drill bit or carbide teeth wearing away. The company defines the process as rock ablation with zero contact, and that’s where the advantage lies. The deeper you go, the hotter and harder the rock becomes; this is precisely where traditional drilling begins to fail.According to Quaise’s July update, the company drilled over 100 meters of granite at a test site in Central Texas, and is now approaching 1 kilometre in depth at the same location, which it refers to as the deepest feat achieved by contactless drilling. The leap from there to more than 5 km in Oregon is substantial, and the company acknowledges this in its timeline.Why a superhot rockTraditional geothermal energy works with hot water or steam at moderate temperatures, near volcanoes or geological fault lines. The thesis of superhot geothermal energy is different: to descend to where rock exceeds 374 °C and water reaches a supercritical state, which carries far more energy per kilogram than regular steam. Thus, a single superhot well can deliver several times what a conventional geothermal well produces. Quaise targets rock at temperatures between 300 °C and 500 °C and at depths that, in most parts of the world, exceed 5 km.What makes Oregon special is the gradient. According to ThinkGeoEnergy, the area leased by Quaise lies south of the Newberry volcano, right next to the border of the Newberry National Volcanic Monument. It spans 1,334 acres within the Deschutes National Forest, featuring a geothermal gradient of about 100 °C per kilometre. In other words, temperatures that elsewhere would require 10 kilometres of drilling are found there at a fraction of the depth. The target reservoirs for Phase I are described at 315 °C and 365 °C.The plan published in April outlines two sets of wells, each with one injector and two producers, and two generating units connected side by side. Phase I is set to deliver 50 MW, with power expected on the grid by 2030; Phase II aims for 250 MW, with the company discussing gigawatt-scale in the long term. For now, the initial wells employ conventional drilling to penetrate the surface layer; the gyrotron will only come into play when the goal is the hotter basement rock at 365 °C, as Quaise explained to the publication.For Brazil, the interesting development is Nabors’ entry. The drilling company operates rigs in various markets, and the combination of a conventional rig for the shallow part with a gyrotron for the hot section is a model that could operate in any sedimentary basin with a favourable gradient, without relying on a volcano. The country hardly explores geothermal energy, partly because there is little hot rock near the surface. If the technology proves successful, depth will no longer be an obstacle, and what will matter is having the rig, team, and regulations ready.Anthony Petrello, president and CEO of Nabors, summarised the logic in the statement by saying that millimetre wave technology changes the equation by reaching superhot rocks at depths beyond the reach of conventional methods. Carlos Araque, CEO and president of Quaise, spoke about unlocking the world’s most powerful clean energy source.A previous experimentA discussion about deep drilling inevitably references the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia. Soviet scientists began in 1970 and reached 12,262 meters by 1989, making it the deepest hole ever drilled, with just a 23-centimetre diameter. What halted progress was not the rock, but the heat. Temperatures at the bottom exceeded 180 °C, well above what models predicted. Under those conditions, the rock behaved more like plastic than solid. The project was abandoned in 1994 due to lack of funds and drill bits capable of withstanding the conditions.It’s clear why the idea of vaporising rock instead of scraping it generates such interest. Kola took nearly two decades to traverse 12 kilometres in still relatively cool rock. Quaise aims to work in rock three times hotter, arguing that millimetre waves are unaffected by the target’s hardness or temperature. It’s a bold promise, and the company still needs to prove that the beam remains stable and efficient well beyond Texas tests.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Footage of Tibet floods isn't being shown in China - and we know little about victims there
articles.summary: Some of the most dramatic footage from the deadly flash flooding is hidden from public view in China.
articles.body:
Watch: China censors videos showing deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border

The dramatic footage was almost impossible to miss. A torrent of water tearing through Gyirong Port, one of the main border crossings between Nepal and Tibet, sweeping away all in its path as hundreds of people fled for their lives.

The scenes, captured by CCTV cameras, quickly spread on social media and onto screens around the world.

Only a single still-frame shot has been broadcast so far by the country's state-run flagship news bulletin.

It has also been difficult to find the full video on China's heavily censored internet. Although various aspects of the disaster have been discussed online.

But what is even harder to find is any first-hand accounts of survivors describing the flash flooding that has claimed hundreds of lives, with just as many still unaccounted for since Wednesday.

Beijing has launched a massive rescue operation involving hundreds of emergency workers, which is continuing, and President Xi Jinping chaired an emergency meeting with officials to co-ordinate efforts.

But when you compare the country's internet content to what much of the world has been seeing online these past few days, China's firewall becomes more visible than ever.

Tibet, which Beijing annexed in the 1950s, had long resisted rule by the Chinese Communist Party.

China has quashed protests over the years, sometimes violently, and has been accused of grave rights violations in the Buddhist region. It has labelled the exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, a separatist.

That history means the very name Tibet draws China's censors. Beijing's sensitivities are especially apparent at times likes this.

Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border

There have been daily updates on the missing and the dead, and Beijing has also been posting updates on the rescue operations, as well as the dangers posed by a barrier lake that has been at risk of overflowing.

On Saturday, new footage from Chinese state media showed rescue teams wandering in a wasteland of mud and rock while calling out to anyone trapped.

But there is little detail beyond that. There are no accounts from survivors in Tibet, and almost no user-generated footage showing the deadly moments or their aftermath.

We are yet to hear from anxious families of those missing. Trying to contact people there is near-impossible during regular times.

As a journalist who has covered North Korea, it has often been easier for me to contact interviewees in Pyongyang than it is in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa.

On Thursday night, as global headlines led on the devastation in a Himalayan valley, China's state broadcaster opened its main bulletin with the launch of Xi's new book, a selection of his "most important and fundamental works".

Foreign journalists cannot travel to Tibet without government permission. We have just a few hours to get as much information as we can on huge stories like this before videos are scrubbed and voices stifled.

Instead, we have to rely on state media, which has so far focused on incredibly dramatic rescue efforts.

Specialist search teams scaling mountains and cliff faces, or crossing raging rivers to try to get to the worst-affected areas. We don't yet know what happened afterwards, or who they were able to save.

This is not to say that Beijing is unconcerned. Rather, they are very concerned.

China's Premier Li Qiang was quickly despatched to the region, where he was seen inspecting debris removal - a rare visit by the country's second-most important leader so soon after a major disaster.

The reason for what the world might see as a muted response is to preserve the one thing Xi covets for his country: stability.

The Communist Party will fear that such a disaster could fuel discontent, either with the response or the lack of foresight to prevent it.

It may also fear the impact of a tragedy like this and its potential to be a rallying factor, especially in a community where faith has long played a central role.

Although the region has not seen protests in a long time, Tibetan groups abroad have expressed concern over increasing Chinese control, such as new education laws that they say aim to weaken the role of monasteries and the Buddhist faith.

Just hours after the disaster struck, the Communist Party machine tried to rally its grassroots to stem any signs of discontent of its handling of the landslide.

A notice came from the local party office urging members to step up and help in disaster relief efforts in their area and provide emotional guidance or psychological support to affected residents.

The key line instructs them to "make every effort to maintain social order and ensure stability and public confidence in the disaster areas". Those who perform well would be rewarded - and those who do badly "would be held accountable".

It is a warning that will not be taken lightly. Tibetans in the region can be detained or arrested for speaking to journalists or posting anything online that is seen as contrary to the government narrative, according to rights activists.

That is making it difficult for Tibetans outside the region to find out what has happened to their relatives.

The International Campaign for Tibet, while praising the work of first responders in the area, said Beijing had been removing videos and other first-hand information from social media. It called on Chinese authorities to "disclose complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".

To try to understand what life is like for Tibetans, the BBC travelled to a town that sits on the edge of the Himalayan plateau last year - just outside what China calls the Tibetan Autonomous region.

There, we spoke to monks at the Kirti monastery in Aba, or Ngaba in Tibetan, which was once at the heart of its resistance to Beijing. "We Tibetans are denied basic human rights," one monk told us.

They said they lived under constant surveillance and claimed the Chinese government oppressed and persecuted Tibetans. The conversations were brief because we could not be seen speaking to anyone for long.

Beijing denies it is violating Tibetans' rights, and points to the heavy investments it has made in the region to boost tourism and integrate it with the rest of the country.

Nevertheless, people in China will not know very much about what is happening in Tibet right now.
